bibl.title: Complementary control of sensory adaptation by two types of cortical interneurons

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: which cortical cells make a neuron respond less to a frequent tone than to a rare one, and by what mechanism each does it
span.quote: We hypothesized that the two most common types of interneurons in the cortex, parvalbumin- (PVs) and somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) ( Xu et al., 2010 ; Rudy et al., 2011 ), facilitate SSA in excitatory neurons of A1 in a complementary fashion.

span.label: whether interneuron types that are hypothesized to have complementary functions actually drive changes in dynamic auditory processing, which had not been established
span.quote: While different interneuron types have been hypothesized to carry out specialized complementary functions in sensory processing ( DeFelipe, 2002 ; Markram et al., 2004 ; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011 ; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014 ; Marlin et al., 2015 ), their function in driving changes in dynamic auditory processing has not been previously established.

span.label: two interneuron types that both amplify the same adaptation index, one by uniform inhibition and one by tone-selective suppression
span.quote: We found that two types of cortical interneurons differentially amplify SSA in putative excitatory neurons. Parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVs) amplify SSA by providing non-specific inhibition: optogenetic suppression of PVs led to an equal increase in responses to frequent and rare tones. In contrast, somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) selectively reduce excitatory responses to frequent tones: suppression of SOMs led to an increase in responses to frequent, but not to rare tones. A mutually coupled excitatory-inhibitory network model accounts for distinct mechanisms by which cortical inhibitory neurons enhance the brain's sensitivity to unexpected sounds.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We found that two types of cortical interneurons differentially amplify SSA in putative excitatory neurons.

span.label: stimulus-specific adaptation in primary auditory cortex
span.quote: The majority of neurons in the primary auditory cortex exhibit SSA, yet little is known about the underlying cortical circuits.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We recorded spiking activity of neurons as well as local field potentials (LFPs) in A1 in head-fixed mice under light isoflurane anesthesia.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A constant PV-derived inhibitory drive, passed through the pyramidal neuron's non-linear synaptic-input-to-firing-rate function, multiplies the effect of thalamocortical synaptic depression on the repeated (standard) tone
span.quote: Taking into account the non-linear synaptic input to FR output function of a typical pyramidal neuron, the constant inhibition amplifies the effect of thalamocortical depression in suppressing the response of the neuron to repeated stimulus ( Figure 7A ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Deviant-tone drive sits on the saturating part of the SOM-to-excitatory transfer function while standard-tone and spontaneous drive sit on its linear part, so SOM modulation can only move the standard
span.quote: The deviant tone-evoked activity falls on the saturating part of the input–output transfer function, whereas the standard tone-evoked and spontaneous inputs fall on the linear part of the transfer function.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because of that operating-point difference, removing SOM inhibition shifts excitatory activity a lot during standard and spontaneous periods but barely at all during the deviant
span.quote: Then, shifts in SOM inputs due to photosuppression evoke small changes during deviant tone responses, but larger changes during either standard or spontaneous activity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An inhibitory circuit element that itself adapts can nevertheless increase adaptation downstream in the excitatory population
span.quote: More generally, the simulation demonstrates that a circuit element, such as PVs or SOMs, that itself adapts may further amplify adaptation in the excitatory neurons.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An equal absolute rise in firing rate is proportionally smaller for the already-larger deviant response, so uniform PV disinhibition compresses the deviant/standard ratio and lowers the SSA index
span.quote: Because an equal increase in the FR produces a weaker relative effect on the response to the deviant (which is higher than to the standard), PV inactivation decreases SSA index ( Figure 3E ).

span.label: PVs may amplify adaptation BY PROVIDING A CONSTANT INHIBITORY DRIVE - EQUALLY STRONG INHIBITORY DRIVE WOULD ATTENUATE THE WEAK RESPONSE TO STANDARD TONES RELATIVELY MORE THAN THE STRONG RESPONSE TO DEVIANT TONES, leading to a greater differential
span.quote: PVs, a subset of which receive direct thalamic inputs ( Staiger et al., 1996 ), may amplify SSA in excitatory neurons by providing a constant inhibitory drive; equally strong inhibitory drive would attenuate the weak response to standard tones relatively more than the strong response to deviant tones, leading to a greater differential between standard vs deviant tone spiking response.

span.label: and SOMs, which TARGET DISTAL DENDRITES and have synapses that EXHIBIT FACILITATION UPON REPETITIVE STIMULATION, may exert A STIMULUS-SPECIFIC INCREASE IN SUPPRESSION that is SELECTIVE TO THE STANDARD TONE AND DOES NOT GENERALIZE TO THE DEVIANT
span.quote: SOMs, which target distal dendrites of pyramidal cells ( McGarry et al., 2010 ; Gentet et al., 2012 ), have excitatory synapses that exhibit facilitation upon repetitive stimulation ( Reyes et al., 1998 ; Silberberg and Markram, 2007 ). Therefore, inputs from SOMs may exert a stimulus-specific increase in suppression of excitatory neurons that is selective to the standard tone and does not generalize to the deviant tone. Alternatively, they may contribute to selective adaptation in excitatory neurons through differential post-synaptic integration.

span.label: with the thalamic input already adapting - the CSD SINK AMPLITUDE WAS LOWER FOR THE STANDARD AS COMPARED TO THE DEVIANT TONES, so excitatory signals produced by THALAMO-CORTICAL INPUTS EXHIBIT SSA
span.quote: We compared the amplitude of the CSD sink for each tone when presented as a deviant or standard, and computed their ratio ( Figure 1F ). The sink amplitude was lower for the standard as compared to the deviant tones ( Figure 1F,G ), suggesting that excitatory signals produced by thalamo-cortical inputs exhibit SSA, consistent with previous findings ( Szymanski et al., 2009 ).

span.label: All recordings were made under light isoflurane anesthesia, so extrapolation to the awake animal is uncertain.
span.quote: One must be cautious in translating the data from our experiments as a strict description of neuronal activity in awake animals, as our results were based on recordings from mice under light isoflurane anesthesia.

span.label: Cell-type identification of the recorded 'putative excitatory' population could not be refined by spike-waveform analysis.
span.quote: The low impedance of the extracellular probes precluded us from conducting a more detailed analysis of cortical subpopulations based on the spike waveform ( Bartho et al., 2004 ; Moore and Wehr, 2013 ).

span.label: Recording site assignment to A1 is not exact; neighboring auditory field data may be included.
span.quote: While the electrodes were targeted to A1, some recordings may include data from the anterior auditory field, adjacent to A1 ( Linden et al., 2003 ).

span.label: The behavioural consequence of the interneuron-mediated adaptation was not measured.
span.quote: However, whether and how modulating SSA in the auditory cortex affects auditory behavior has not yet been tested.

span.label: The interpretation of the firing-rate differences as synaptic transfer functions carries explicitly acknowledged caveats.
span.quote: There are several caveats to this interpretation.

span.label: THE FR MAY NOT LINEARLY TRANSLATE ONTO SYNAPTIC INPUT STRENGTH because of THE SPIKING NON-LINEAR RECTIFICATION between the inputs and outputs of the putative excitatory neuron
span.quote: There are several caveats to this interpretation. First, the FR may not linearly translate onto synaptic input strength because of the spiking non-linear rectification between the inputs and outputs of the putative excitatory neuron

span.label: the results are from mice UNDER LIGHT ISOFLURANE ANESTHESIA, and OTHER FORMS OF ANESTHESIA can affect the measurements
span.quote: in awake animals, as our results were based on recordings from mice under light isoflurane anesthesia. Other forms of anesthesia, such as pentobarbital-based ( Cheung et al., 2001 ; Gaese and Ostwald, 2001 ), ketamine ( Otazu et al., 2009 ) and high concentrations of isoflurane ( Cheung et al., 2001 ; Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2007 ), can affect multiple

span.label: the excitatory neurons are PUTATIVE - identified by response pattern and the absence of light suppression, and THE LOW IMPEDANCE OF THE EXTRACELLULAR PROBES PRECLUDED a more detailed analysis based on the spike waveform
span.quote: Putative excitatory neurons were identified based on their expected response patterns to sounds and the lack of significant suppression of the spontaneous FR due to light ( Lima et al., 2009 ; Moore and Wehr, 2013 ). While this subpopulation may still contain inhibitory neurons, only 2% of all recorded neurons were significantly photosuppressed at baseline (one-sided paired t-test, significance taken at p < 0.05). The low impedance of the extracellular probes precluded us from conducting a more detailed analysis of cortical subpopulations based on the spike waveform

span.label: whether this circuit affects behaviour is left open - FUTURE EXPERIMENTS WILL EXPLORE WHETHER INTERNEURON-MEDIATED SSA INDEED AFFECTS THE AUDITORY BEHAVIOR OF THE SUBJECT
span.quote: By combining optogenetic manipulation of interneuron activity with behavioral measurements, future experiments will explore whether interneuron-mediated SSA indeed affects the auditory behavior of the subject, such as enhanced ability to detect unexpected events.

span.label: the idea that adapting to context increases coding efficiency under limited resources, used as the reason adaptation should exist at all
span.quote: Whereas SSA has also been found in sub-cortical structures e.g. in the auditory midbrain ( Malmierca et al., 2009 ; Zhao et al., 2011 ; Thomas et al., 2012 ) and the auditory thalamus ( Kraus et al., 1994 ; Anderson et al., 2009 ; Antunes et al., 2010 ; Bauerle et al., 2011 ), it is weak in the lemniscal areas of the auditory pathway, which project to A1, and stronger in those non-lemniscal areas which receive feedback from A1 ( Ulanovsky et al., 2004 , Perez-Gonzalez et al., 2005 , Duque et al., 2012 ). Therefore, cortical circuits are proposed to contribute to and amplify SSA in A1 ( Ulanovsky et al., 2003 , Szymanski et al., 2009 , Bauerle et al., 2011 , Fishman and Steinschneider, 2012 , Escera and Malmierca, 2014 ), through a combination of plastic modulation of thalamocortical inputs and intra-cortical inhibitory circuits, which would allow for selective suppression of neuronal responses to specific stimuli ( Nelken, 2014 ).

span.label: a mutually coupled excitatory-inhibitory population model, built specifically to reconcile equal adaptation in both interneuron types with unequal effects on the excitatory cells
span.quote: As a proof-of-principle that would account for our findings that PVs and SOMs exhibit similar magnitude of SSA, yet have a differential effect on SSA in putative excitatory neurons, we constructed a simplified model of mutually coupled inhibitory–excitatory neuronal populations

span.label: the analysis restricted to subpopulations MATCHED ON MEAN AND STANDARD DEVIATION of the firing rate to standard against deviant tones
span.quote: However, restricting the analysis to two subpopulations of neurons, which have matched mean and standard deviation of FR to the standard vs the deviant tones ( Ulanovsky et al., 2004 ; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010 ), preserved the observed

span.label: the same comparison run on the strong against the weak tone rather than standard against deviant
span.quote: However, PV and SOM suppression exhibited a similar effect on responses to the strong and the weak tones in neurons that exhibited differential responses to two tones ( Figure 4—figure supplements 5, 6 ).

span.label: the normalization redone against the mean rather than the maximum firing rate
span.quote: FR normalization was carried out separately for each tone, A and B, for each neuron by dividing the response under all conditions by the maximum FR (across 5-ms bins) of the deviant tone, light-off condition. Performing this normalization by dividing response in all conditions by the mean, rather than maximum FR of the deviant tone, light-off condition did not alter significant results ( Figure 4—figure supplement 8 ).

span.label: the caveat about spiking non-linearity worked through rather than left standing
span.quote: However, our findings would still hold were this the case: in examining the effect of SOM suppression on response to the deviant, the actual difference in the synaptic drive between the deviant and the standard would then be even greater

span.label: TWO CELL TYPES AMPLIFY THE SAME INDEX BY OPPOSITE MECHANISMS: PVs AMPLIFY SSA BY PROVIDING NON-SPECIFIC INHIBITION - suppression led to AN EQUAL INCREASE IN RESPONSES TO FREQUENT AND RARE TONES - while SOMs SELECTIVELY REDUCE EXCITATORY RESPONSES TO FREQUENT TONES, with suppression increasing responses TO FREQUENT, BUT NOT TO RARE TONES
span.quote: We found that two types of cortical interneurons differentially amplify SSA in putative excitatory neurons. A mutually coupled excitatory-inhibitory network model accounts for distinct mechanisms by which cortical inhibitory neurons enhance the brain's sensitivity to unexpected sounds.

span.label: AND THE FIRST MECHANISM MOVES THE INDEX WITHOUT CHANGING SELECTIVITY AT ALL: one type SUPPRESSED RESPONSES TO BOTH FREQUENT AND RARE SOUNDS, and AS THE RESPONSES TO RARE SOUNDS STARTED OFF GREATER, SUPPRESSING BOTH BY AN EQUAL AMOUNT ACTUALLY LED TO AN INCREASE IN THE RELATIVE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM. A ratio moved by a uniform shift, and the paper says so in its own summary
span.quote: One of these neuron types, called ‘parvalbumin-positive interneurons’, exerted a general effect on excitatory neurons and suppressed responses to both frequent and rare sounds As the responses to rare sounds started off greater than the responses to frequent sounds, suppressing both by an equal amount actually led to an increase in the relative difference between them.

span.label: with the arithmetic stated as the hypothesis before it is tested: EQUALLY STRONG INHIBITORY DRIVE WOULD ATTENUATE THE WEAK RESPONSE TO STANDARD TONES RELATIVELY MORE THAN THE STRONG RESPONSE TO DEVIANT TONES, LEADING TO A GREATER DIFFERENTIAL - the effect is predicted from the shape of the index rather than from a property of the cell
span.quote: PVs, a subset of which receive direct thalamic inputs ( Staiger et al., 1996 ), may amplify SSA in excitatory neurons by providing a constant inhibitory drive; equally strong inhibitory drive would attenuate the weak response to standard tones relatively more than the strong response to deviant tones, leading to a greater differential between standard vs deviant tone spiking response.

span.quote: SOMs, which target distal dendrites of pyramidal cells ( McGarry et al., 2010 ; Gentet et al., 2012 ), have excitatory synapses that exhibit facilitation upon repetitive stimulation ( Reyes et al., 1998 ; Silberberg and Markram, 2007 ). Therefore, inputs from SOMs may exert a stimulus-specific increase in suppression of excitatory neurons that is selective to the standard tone and does not generalize to the deviant tone. Alternatively, they may contribute to selective adaptation in excitatory neurons through differential post-synaptic integration.

span.label: THE INDEX IS DEFINED WITH ITS TWO ENDPOINTS: SSA index is 1 WHEN ADAPTATION IS COMPLETE, no response to the standard and significant response to the deviant, AND 0 WHEN THERE IS NO ADAPTATION, the response to the standard and deviant equal
span.quote: To quantify the level of adaptation for each neuron, we computed the index of the change in FR to the same tone when it was presented as the deviant vs the standard (SSA index). SSA index is 1 when adaptation is complete (i.e., no response to the standard, and significant response to the deviant), and 0 when there is no adaptation (i.e., the response to the standard and deviant is equal).

span.label: and written out as a formula whose numerator is a difference and whose denominator is a sum - which is exactly why a uniform multiplicative change moves it
span.quote: For each neuron, SSA index is a measure of the strength of SSA based on its mean FR with respect to tone probability. FRs to tones A and B were summed according to their standard or deviant probability within each oddball stimulus ( Ulanovsky et al., 2003 ). Thus, SSA index was computed as: S S A I n d e x = ( D A + D B ) − ( S A + S B ) D A + D B + S A + S B , where S and D indicate the mean FR for standard and deviant trials, respectively, and their subscripts indicate the tone frequency condition.

span.label: A BASELINE-DIFFERENCE CONFOUND CONTROLLED BY MATCHING RATHER THAN BY ARGUMENT: restricting the analysis to subpopulations WHICH HAVE MATCHED MEAN AND STANDARD DEVIATION OF FR TO THE STANDARD VS THE DEVIANT TONES preserved the observation
span.quote: However, restricting the analysis to two subpopulations of neurons, which have matched mean and standard deviation of FR to the standard vs the deviant tones ( Ulanovsky et al., 2004 ; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010 ), preserved the observed

span.label: and the same test run on a different contrast: PV AND SOM SUPPRESSION EXHIBITED A SIMILAR EFFECT ON RESPONSES TO THE STRONG AND THE WEAK TONES in neurons that responded differentially to the two tones - so the selectivity is to probability, not to response size
span.quote: However, PV and SOM suppression exhibited a similar effect on responses to the strong and the weak tones in neurons that exhibited differential responses to two tones ( Figure 4—figure supplements 5, 6 ).

span.label: with the normalization choice checked rather than assumed: dividing by the MEAN rather than the MAXIMUM firing rate DID NOT ALTER SIGNIFICANT RESULTS
span.quote: FR normalization was carried out separately for each tone, A and B, for each neuron by dividing the response under all conditions by the maximum FR (across 5-ms bins) of the deviant tone, light-off condition. Performing this normalization by dividing response in all conditions by the mean, rather than maximum FR of the deviant tone, light-off condition did not alter significant results ( Figure 4—figure supplement 8 ).

span.label: A CAVEAT WORKED THROUGH INSTEAD OF LEFT STANDING: THE FR MAY NOT LINEARLY TRANSLATE ONTO SYNAPTIC INPUT STRENGTH because of the SPIKING NON-LINEAR RECTIFICATION - and OUR FINDINGS WOULD STILL HOLD WERE THIS THE CASE, since the actual difference in synaptic drive WOULD THEN BE EVEN GREATER
span.quote: However, our findings would still hold were this the case: in examining the effect of SOM suppression on response to the deviant, the actual difference in the synaptic drive between the deviant and the standard would then be even greater

span.label: with the method chosen against its predecessors on a stated ground: optogenetic methods OVERCOME THE LIMITATIONS OF LESION OR PHARMACOLOGICAL STUDIES, WHICH ONLY ALLOW FOR PROLONGED, NON-SELECTIVE INACTIVATION
span.quote: optogenetic methods to test the function of inhibitory interneurons in SSA overcomes the limitations of lesion or pharmacological studies ( Elliott and Trahiotis, 1972 ; Duque et al., 2014 ), which only allow for prolonged, non-selective inactivation ( Moore et al., 2001 ).
